text:
The Network Engineer Who Hates Programming Just Built an App

I’m holding @artofneteng app in my hands. It hits the App Store soon.

Seven months ago, the network engineer who built it was losing hours to a chatbot, pasting code he didn’t understand and watching it fail. He hates programming. He’ll tell you himself.

Let me tell you how we got from there to here, because I think it’s the most important story I can share with any network engineer who still thinks AI isn’t for them.

7 MONTHS AGO: THE SPARK
@andylapteff, Michael Bushong, and I sat down for “The ABCs of AI.”

I was describing what happens when you connect an AI agent to your source of truth through Model Context Protocol (MCP). No spreadsheets. No jump box. Just ask NetBox, in plain English, how many circuits you have in the Phoenix data center.

Andy’s reaction: “If I could have a conversation with my source of truth in natural language... I got tingly. I’m like, ‘Holy sh*t.’” Watch the moment: https://t.co/owZZhluHhB

When I suggested he build that agent himself, so the whole team came to “Andy’s agent” for answers, his reply was instant: “They’re never gonna get rid of me.” [35:57]

Michael reframed the fear that keeps so many of us stuck: “I would be more afraid of not AI than I would of AI.” [11:28]

But Andy was honest about where he was. He’d just lost an hour to ChatGPT trying to pull YouTube transcripts. Code, error. Code, error. And a chatbot cheerfully telling him “we’re almost there.” [45:16] His verdict: “When I vibe code, it’s all bad vibes, man.” [47:03]

THE PUSH
This is where Michael did what good friends do. He signed Andy up on the spot: “Andy, let’s be clear, what he’s basically signing you up for is that you’re going to go through and you’re going to do a hello world and we’re going to record it.” [43:30]

And he explained exactly why a Hello World is the right first step: “It’s super bounded in terms of what can go wrong because it takes away a lot of the fear.” [38:22]

Then, simply: “Andy, let’s do it. Let’s just say yes.” [45:00]

5 MONTHS AGO: HELLO WORLD

“You Don’t Need Python Anymore: Hello World For AI”

Here’s what I need you to understand about this episode: I didn’t drive. Andy shared his screen and did the work. I just talked him through it.

That matters, because he’d already tried the pre-work on his own. His words: “I had to clone a repo and I got scared and I ran away.” [2:17]

So we started right there. I opened by telling him something I meant: “It takes a lot of courage to learn in public like this.” [0:50]

Then he ran his first git clone. Live. On camera. I called for a round of applause, and Andy turned to every network engineer watching and told them that if you can work in the Cisco CLI, “you can work in a VS Code terminal.” [5:24]

Then it broke. The MCP server wouldn’t start. Bad JSON. A virtual environment detour. Andy, laughing, said some people “attract every weird bug... I’m one of them.” [18:00]

He kept going. When the server came up and the NetBox tools appeared in Copilot: “Hot dang.” [21:00]

Then the agent hallucinated and tried to write a Python script instead of using the MCP tool sitting right in front of it. A more explicit prompt fixed it. That’s the job now: guide the agent, then check its work.

Somewhere in the middle of all that JSON, something shifted: “The more I’m exposed to this stuff, the less scary it is.” [26:15]

About half an hour in, he had a CSV of NetBox sites generated from a plain-English request. I told him: “The hello world is successful, Andy. Give yourself a hand, bravo.” [30:20]

His answer: “I think this is the perfect hello world for AI.” [33:20]

Then we did it all again in Claude Desktop, and broke it again. When the config got mangled, my advice was to “just cheat and let the AI fix it for you.” He did. [38:05]

Andy’s attitude toward the friction is the whole lesson: “I have to troubleshoot a bit. It’s no big deal.” [43:40]

And his wrap-up is the line I want every engineer in the 70% to hear: “It’s not coding... when the JSON was wrong, the agent fixed it.” “We got this working in like 30-ish minutes.” Watch it: https://t.co/0kqUOOznPx

Two months from “holy sh*t” to his first real build.

THE KEY: ANDY DID IT HIMSELF
Andy opened that episode by admitting “the coding stuff, the dev stuff, it’s been painful for me.” Then he said how he deals with it: “you just keep your head down, you learn, you push through.” [1:30]

That’s the difference. Thousands of people have watched someone else do an AI demo. Watching didn’t change their careers. Andy put his own hands on the keyboard.

Every network engineer already knows this. Nobody passed the CCNA by watching someone else configure OSPF. You lab it. You break it. You fix it. The reps are the learning.

Andy said it himself at the end: “This is your home lab. So try it out.” [48:15]

And that’s how the ball starts rolling. The first git clone is terrifying. The tenth is boring. The first broken JSON eats twenty minutes. The next one, you hand to the agent. Before we even signed off, Andy was already asking how to bring this into his day job. My answer: “Be the AI expert in your shop.” [48:45]

Which is why, a few months later in Munich, he didn’t need me holding the keyboard.

1 MONTH AGO: FROM VIBES TO SPECS
“Stop Vibe Coding: Start Spec-Driven Development”

At AutoCon 5 in Munich, Andy and I sat down again. Live, unrehearsed, no prep, and Andy at the keyboard. This time the topic was Spec-Driven Development (SDD) using GitHub’s open-source Spec Kit with Claude Code. 14,000 of you watched. https://t.co/RDj2aq16hZ

By then, the ball was already rolling. Andy had been building things in Claude Code on his own, including a website. But he was still vibe coding: ask for something, hope it runs. In his words: “I think if it works, I’m happy.” [43:36]

SDD is what vibe coding grows up into. Six steps, and every one produces a Markdown file that lives in Git right next to your code:

Constitution: the guardrails and principles every line of code has to respect. Specify: the what and the why. User stories, requirements, acceptance criteria. No tech stack yet. Clarify: the AI reads your constitution and spec, then asks you up to five questions about what you missed. Plan: now you choose the tech stack and architecture. Tasks: the plan broken into dependency-ordered work. Implement: the code gets written, tested, and fixed until the tests pass.

Sound familiar? It should. As I put it to Andy: “What do you do for a network change? You gather requirements, right?” [2:51] Implementation plan. Test plan. Rollback plan. Success criteria. Network engineers have been doing SDD for years. We just never called it a spec.

Andy got it in one line: “This is the thing we need, and this is the plan to get there.” [3:23]

Before we even wrote the spec, I told Andy about the step that makes SDD different from everything he’d been doing: clarify. Once the spec exists, you don’t start coding. You ask the AI whether anything is unclear, and it comes back with questions for you, the human. [14:35]

That’s when Andy stopped and looked back at everything he’d been building in Claude Code. He asked: “Should this be my new way forward for things I built?” I said yes. And he saw why right away: “This is more structured than what I’ve been doing.” This is the moment it clicked: https://t.co/8WHNPHKAsL

Somewhere in the spec, Claude described our game as a typing tutor “like Duolingo, but for subnetting.” [17:02] Andy’s first reaction: “oh my God, we could get rich.” [17:28] His second was more honest: “I had such a hard time learning subnetting.” [17:43]

Then we ran /speckit.clarify for real. I described it the way I’d describe handing a spec to someone on my team: “This is kind of like your junior, right?” Review it, and come back to me with questions before you do anything else. [25:19]

Andy watched it start working through our constitution and spec, and this is what came out of him:

“This is crazy in the best way possible.”

“I can’t believe what I’m seeing happening in front of me.”

“I would never have got to the point where I could do this.”

[25:24]

Read that again, and remember where he started. Seven months earlier, a chatbot was telling Andy “we’re almost there” while his code broke over and over. Now an AI was doing the opposite. Before writing a single line, it stopped and asked him what he meant.

And look at what it asked. Between the spec and clarify steps, Claude came back with questions neither of us had thought to answer. Who is this for? IPv4 only, or IPv6 too? Multiple choice or free text? What counts as mastery before you unlock the next tier? How should the game teach a concept before testing it? Should there be time pressure?

Not one of those is a coding question. They’re design review questions. And Andy had the answers, because they come from knowing the subject and knowing the people you’re building for. He said those words as someone who never thought he’d have access to software development, and in that moment he realized the door had never been locked by code. It had been locked by the assumption that you need to write code to build software.

That’s why it baffled him. Clarify flips the relationship. The AI isn’t a magic box you hope gets it right, and it isn’t a developer you have to become. It’s a junior engineer that brings its questions to you before it touches anything. For a network engineer who has spent a career in change reviews, that’s home turf.

Clarify is where a network engineer stops being the person who can’t code and becomes the person whose judgment the code depends on.

Then we hit implement. As I said on the episode: “We haven’t written a single line of code. Everything has been in Markdown.” [42:26] And Andy, borrowing from Scott Robohn, reminded everyone that none of this means giving up networking: “it’s all additive... It doesn’t go away.” [42:52]

Eric Chou wandered in mid-build and summed up life with AI in one line: “I don’t feel like I get stuck anymore.” [44:53]

Then SDD did the thing vibe coding never did for Andy. It tested itself. It wrote failing tests first, then fixed the code until they passed. Andy watched it happen: “it’s testing the hell out of the code.” [48:06]

By the end: 77 tests, all green, and 100% coverage on the subnetting engine, before either of us had even touched the game. [56:10] Why does that matter? Because, as I said on the episode, “that kid who does the subnet game and it tells them the wrong answer, that’s on us.” [56:38]

Andy laughed that we were “apologizing that it took an hour to do like a year’s worth of work.” [51:34]

THEN ANDY BUILT THE APP
Here’s the part I most want you to hear.

Andy didn’t leave Munich with a subnetting game. He left with a method. And then he went home and used it to build The Art of Network Engineering app.

I wrote the initial spec. Andy wrote every spec after that. Not me. Andy. Constitution, specify, clarify, plan, tasks, implement: the same six steps he learned on camera, applied to his own show’s app. The constitution, spec, plan, and tasks live in the repo right next to the code, so anyone can see exactly how it was built.

My favorite detail? The project’s constitution says no feature counts as “done” until it’s been verified on a real device. That’s change discipline. That’s a network engineer’s instinct, written into a spec.

Vibe coding gave Andy something that might run. SDD gave him something he could build on, test, and hand to a community.

TODAY
That’s the app I’m holding right now. And the “Duolingo for subnetting” game from Munich? It’s in there too, one of many community resources at your fingertips. In your pocket. On your phone. Think about that.

Was Andy a programmer? No. And that’s fine. Let’s not judge Andy because he grew up on the CLI instead of the IDE. So did most of us.

He didn’t become a developer. He embraced a few simple, easy-to-follow tools and methods: a protocol, a source of truth, and a spec. And he did the reps himself. Look what that built.

7 months. 5 months. 1 month. Today.

WHAT THIS MEANS FOR YOU
Michael said something in The ABCs of AI that I can’t stop thinking about: “If you get there early, it’s a lottery ticket. It’s opportunity. If you’re the last one to the party... the keg’s going to be empty.” [37:57] And: “The faster this train goes, the harder it is to jump on while it’s moving.” [38:08]

The good news is that the on-ramp has never been shorter. As Michael put it: “Your ideas have never been more accessible than they are today. And every day they’ll be more accessible than they were the day before.” [42:28]

Andy’s path is a map you can follow:

Find your “tingly” question. What do people ask you every week that sends you digging through spreadsheets, SharePoint, and jump boxes? That’s your first use case.
Do the Hello World yourself. Don’t just watch it. Andy’s first git clone happened on camera, and so did his first broken JSON. Use the NetBox demo instance, connect the MCP server, and stay read-only. When you hit errors, paste them back to the AI and ask it to explain. Use AI to help you with AI.
Write a spec, not a prompt. If you can write a MOP or a change request, you can write a spec. Install Spec Kit, walk all six steps on a side project, and let the clarify step show you what you missed. Want a head start? Take my advice from Munich: “Do BGP as a video game. OSPF as a video game. Open source it.” [27:05] The Networking Game Starter Kit is here: https://t.co/cg3WEEmrRY
Build the thing people come to you for. Andy’s agent. Andy’s app. That’s not automating yourself out of a job. That’s becoming the person nobody can imagine the team without.
Find your Michael. Someone who’ll say “let’s just say yes” and then hold you to it.

One last quote from Michael: “Not everybody gets off the couch, right? But you can, and it doesn’t have to be super scary.” [38:57]

What’s your Hello World going to be?

YOU WON’T BE DOING IT ALONE
If you get stuck on your own Hello World, or you want to walk through Spec-Driven Development on something of yours, come find us in the VibeOps Forum, a free, open Slack workspace for practitioners: https://t.co/UDEmp2hdwk

Andy and I are both in there, and we’re both happy to help you directly. Ask the question you think is too basic. Paste the error you’re embarrassed by. Share the spec you’re not sure about. Nobody is going to judge you for where you’re starting from. Andy asked every question out loud, on camera, and look where it got him.

ABOUT THAT APP
AONE Mobile is the official iPhone and Apple Watch companion for The Art of Network Engineering. Here’s what you’ll have in your pocket:

Every podcast episode, with background audio, resume-where-you-left-off, real show notes, and tappable guest chips
Every video, playing right inside the app
Every blog post, searchable and readable on your phone
AONE’s full resource catalog: 154 curated links across 21 categories, from certifications and courses to communities and books
Every guest who’s ever been on the show, with every episode they’ve appeared in
One search box across episodes, videos, guests, and resources
Live community stats and a one-tap button into the Discord
Merch, the newsletter, and ways to support the show
Apple Watch controls for whatever episode is playing

Here’s why this community should be excited. Nearly everything in the app reads live from AONE’s own public GitHub repo, the same source as the website. No separate silo. No stale copy. When AONE publishes, it flows into your pocket.

But the bigger thing is what the app represents. For years, this community has been the place where people cheer each other on when they pass and pick each other up when they fail an exam. Now that travels with you. A study resource on the train. An episode on the drive in. The guest who went through exactly what you’re going through, one tap away. The Discord, one tap away.

Andy said it at the end of The ABCs of AI, the episode that started all of this: “You don’t have to trudge this road alone.” [52:40]

And the app itself is proof of everything in this post. Andy built it with the same six steps this community watched him learn, live, on camera, at AutoCon 5.

Seven months ago, Andy was getting gaslit by a chatbot. Today, he’s built an app that puts this whole community in your pocket.

Coming soon to the App Store.
